source.title_on_document: Can You Make It Sound Like You? Post-Editing LLM-Generated Text for Personal Style

supplement.where: Appendices A-D, PDF pp. 13-29. No separate supplementary PDF is identified in the document.
supplement.holds: Appendix A gives recruitment, exclusions and permutation-test details (pp. 13-14). Appendix B includes embedding-model robustness results with g and confidence intervals (Table 3, p. 16), exploratory mixed-effects coefficients and standard errors (Tables 4-6, p. 18; Table 8, p. 21), and linguistic-acceptability results (pp. 20-21). Appendix C reports the separate formative survey (pp. 22-23); Table 9 and Appendix D give task counts and interface details (pp. 24-29). Main H1/H2 g and intervals also appear in the main text; no participant-level standard errors for the main diversity contrasts are supplied.

paper_design_summary: An independent formative survey selected personal writing scenarios using 88 attention-check passers (p. 23, Appendix C). In the main preregistered online within-person study, 81 analyzed Prolific participants completed randomized blocks of unaided writing and post-editing GPT-o4-mini drafts generated from their plans (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1). Outputs were scored using stylistic embeddings, an AI detector and a linguistic-acceptability model, including stylistic similarity across different participants’ texts (pp. 5-7, sections 5-6; p. 21, Appendix B.7.1).

studies.label: Main online within-person personal-writing and post-editing experiment

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each participant completed treatment and control writing blocks, described as randomized in section 4 and Figure 1. Participants selected six writing tasks; four were randomly selected for the AI-draft post-editing block and two for unaided control writing. Randomized block ordering is taken from the paper’s description of two randomized blocks; sequence counts and the allocation algorithm are not supplied.
assignment.quote: As illustrated in Figure 1, participants completed pre- and post-surveys, task difficulty surveys, a brief tutorial, and two randomized writing task blocks (treatment and control).
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9 caption
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1, introduction and footnote 2: https://aspredicted.org/ck6xk4.pdf; p. 3, section 3, main preregistered H1/H2; p. 13, Appendix A.1, preregistered exclusion criteria

arms.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
arms.description: The same analyzed participants supply content plans and edit an automatically generated LLM draft to express their personal style; four selected writing tasks per participant (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). Original unedited LLM drafts are retained as a reference stage, not a separately randomized arm.

arms.name: Unassisted human control writing
arms.description: The same analyzed participants plan and write without seeing any LLM-generated text; two selected writing tasks per participant (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). This is the within-person control block, not a separate participant sample or a delayed follow-up.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 100 recruited and 81 included in the final analysis, not an explicit number randomized at assignment (p. 4, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1). Preregistered exclusions removed people who never edited any LLM draft or did not finish the study; counts by exclusion reason are not given. Recruitment was lower than preregistered because completion took longer than piloting and the authors preserved the intended hourly pay within their budget (p. 13, footnote 13).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific users, limited to one session per person (p. 13, Appendix A.1). All analyzed participants contribute to both conditions; arm counts must not be added.
participants.quote: Using this procedure, we recruit 100 participants of which we include 81 in our final analysis
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1; p. 24, Table 9 caption

ai_tool.how_used: The system automatically supplies a full draft from the participant’s planned bullet-point details and the writing scenario; the participant then post-edits it for personal style (pp. 4-5, sections 4-5.1). This is initial-draft generation followed by human editing, not AI refinement of a human-written draft or free chatbot conversation. The AI-generated draft remains available while the scored treatment output is produced.

task.description: Participants choose six of eight personal writing scenarios and provide fictional planned details. Tasks include thank-you and apology letters, wedding/birthday speeches, catch-up and condolence letters, reassurance/encouragement messages, wedding vows, and eulogies/obituaries/tributes (p. 24, Table 9). Four tasks use AI-draft post-editing and two use unaided writing. Planning requires at least 30 characters; control writing at least 150 characters; the example generation prompt requests about 150 words (pp. 4-5, section 4 and Prompt 4.1).
task.duration: At least two minutes per treatment post-editing task (p. 5, section 4); mean whole-study completion time 1.69 hours (p. 13, Appendix A.1). No separate control-task time limit is stated.

outcomes.name: Across-participant stylistic homogeneity (H2a, H2b)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of LUAR-MUD style embeddings, comparing texts from different participants within each text condition. Higher similarity means less stylistic diversity. CISR is a robustness model, retained within this outcome (p. 5, section 5.2; pp. 6-7, section 6.2 and Figure 6; pp. 14, 16, Appendix B.2 and Table 3). H2 is called a main preregistered hypothesis on p. 3, but no single primary endpoint is designated. This is the main eligible across_people outcome.

contrasts.reported: H2a, stylistic similarity: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = 1.03, 95% CI [0.91, 1.14]. The treatment is less diverse. Printed similarity effects are retained unchanged; direction is reversed to describe diversity. Arm means, SDs and pair counts are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2a

contrasts.control_arm: Original LLM-generated drafts before post-editing (reference stage of treatment)
contrasts.reported: H2b, stylistic similarity: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -0.69, 95% CI [-0.74, -0.63]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.62]. Post-edited text is more diverse than original LLM text. Printed similarity effects are retained unchanged; direction describes diversity. This compares text stages, not separately randomized human groups.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2b

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine stylistic similarity; higher values mean greater homogeneity and lower diversity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: LUAR-MUD (Rivera-Soto et al., 2021); robustness: CISR (Wegmann et al., 2022).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of texts from different participants, separately for the original LLM-generated, post-edited, and unassisted human-control pools (p. 7, Figure 6). Exact pair enumeration, aggregation and analyzed pair counts are not specified. Writing-task reference matching is described where applicable in Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g with 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are printed; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini–Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The participant/block resampling scheme and handling of dependence among text pairs are not stated, so participant-valid precision is not established by this PDF.
diversity_detail.notes: The experimental contrast is post-edited versus unaided human writing. Original LLM drafts are an additional reference stage, not a third randomized arm. Direction is coded for diversity, while reported g and intervals retain the source’s similarity sign. The same people contribute both human conditions.

outcomes.name: Similarity to other participants’ post-edited text versus own unassisted writing (H2c)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Compares the same post-edited output with other participants’ post-edited text and with its author’s unassisted control reference. This is a cross-person stylistic-convergence comparison, not a separate randomized arm contrast. CISR is a robustness measure (p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right; p. 16, Table 3).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited text compared with other participants’ post-edited text
contrasts.control_arm: Same post-edited text compared with the author’s unassisted control text
contrasts.reported: H2c: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = 1.14, 95% CI [1.02, 1.26]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = 2.09, 95% CI [1.94, 2.24]. Post-edited text is more similar to others’ post-edited text than to the author’s own control text. Direction is coded as greater convergence/lower diversity; reported similarity signs are unchanged.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right; p. 16, Table 3, H2c

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine stylistic similarity to other participants’ post-edited text versus similarity to own unassisted control writing.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Post-edited text against other participants’ post-edited references and against the same participant’s control reference. Appendix A.2 describes embedding concatenated control texts and matching reference writing tasks where applicable (pp. 13-14). Exact reference averaging and pair counts for H2c are not given.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g with 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are printed; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini–Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The participant/block resampling scheme and handling of dependence among text pairs are not stated, so participant-valid precision is not established by this PDF.
diversity_detail.notes: The comparator changes the reference source for the same post-edited output. It is not an estimate of a randomized treatment-control difference in pool-wide diversity and should not be pooled as such.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to the author’s own unassisted control writing (H1a)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each treatment text, before and after editing, to an embedding of that participant’s concatenated control texts (p. 13, Appendix A.2). This scores personal stylistic authenticity, not overall creativity or novelty. CISR is a robustness model (p. 16, Table 3); exploratory moderation by perceived style importance is in Table 4 (p. 18). Appendix B.7.3 (p. 22, Figure 13) reports associations of change in this same outcome with edit number/length, rather than additional creative outcomes.

contrasts.control_arm: Original LLM-generated drafts before post-editing (reference stage of treatment)
contrasts.reported: H1a: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = 0.55, 95% CI [0.38, 0.71]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = 0.48, 95% CI [0.32, 0.64]. Exploratory mixed model, Table 4: post-edited (True) estimate = 0.055, SE = 0.006, z = 9.167, p < .001, 95% CI [0.043, 0.066]; post-edited (True) x personal style importance (Non-max) estimate = -0.017, SE = 0.013, z = -1.280, p = .201, 95% CI [-0.042, 0.009].
contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1a; p. 18, Table 4; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Personalized stylistic alignment: own versus other participants’ unassisted references (H1a′)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Tests whether stylistic alignment after post-editing is specific to the author rather than generic human style. Coded other because this compares personal-reference alignment, not an arm-level diversity score. Figure 5 left shows final post-edited text versus own and others’ controls; section 6.1 also describes the result as a difference in stylistic shifts. CISR and the exploratory CoLA-adjusted reference-author model are variants of this endpoint (p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5; p. 16, Table 3; p. 21, Table 8).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited text: similarity to others’ unassisted control writing
contrasts.control_arm: Same post-edited text: similarity to own unassisted control writing
contrasts.reported: H1a′: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.43]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.16]. The text states that editing moves writing more toward the author’s own style than other participants’ styles, and Figure 5 left shows lower similarity to others’ control writing. The printed sign is retained; confirm whether the reported test uses final levels or changes before effect extraction.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1a′

contrasts.reported: Exploratory mixed-effects model predicting change in stylistic similarity, Table 8: reference author (self) estimate = 0.027, SE = 0.004, z = 6.079, p < .001, 95% CI [0.018, 0.035]; CoLA difference estimate = -0.086, SE = 0.031, z = -2.777, p = .005, 95% CI [-0.147, -0.025]; CoLA difference x reference author (self) estimate = -0.116, SE = 0.040, z = -2.931, p = .003, 95% CI [-0.193, -0.038]. These are reference and moderator associations, not randomized aid contrasts.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to LLM-generated reference text (H1b)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between treatment text and other LLM-generated reference text, before and after human editing. Reference writing tasks are matched to the participant’s control tasks where applicable (pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2). CISR is a robustness model; perceived-style-importance moderation is another analysis of the same outcome (p. 16, Table 3; pp. 18-19, Table 5 and Appendix B.5). Pair is used for text-reference comparisons; the PDF does not specify the full reference averaging and independent-unit structure. This is an AI-style indicator rather than a creativity rating.

contrasts.control_arm: Original LLM-generated drafts before post-editing (reference stage of treatment)
contrasts.reported: H1b: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -0.41, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.39]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -0.55, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.53]. Exploratory mixed model, Table 5: post-edited (True) estimate = -0.039, SE = 0.001, z = -41.097, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.041, -0.037]; post-edited (True) x personal style importance (Non-max) estimate = 0.020, SE = 0.002, z = 9.614, p < .001, 95% CI [0.016, 0.024].
contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1b; p. 18, Table 5; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: PANGRAM AI-authorship likelihood (additional H1b measure)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: PANGRAM estimates the likelihood that an individual text is AI-authored (p. 5, section 5.2). It is an additional operational measure of retained AI stylistic traces, with a different scoring model and output-level unit from embedding-reference comparisons. No creativity or diversity interpretation is assigned to the score itself.

contrasts.control_arm: Original LLM-generated drafts before post-editing (reference stage of treatment)

outcomes.name: Relative stylistic similarity to own control writing versus LLM writing (H1c)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Compares the same post-edited text’s similarity to its author’s unassisted reference with its similarity to LLM-generated references. CISR and the exploratory reference-source/style-importance model are variants of this endpoint (p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right; p. 16, Table 3; pp. 18-19, Table 6 and Appendix B.5). This is a reference-source comparison, not AI-assisted versus unaided output quality. Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14) describes reference construction and task matching; exact reference averaging for this test is not stated.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited text compared with own unassisted control reference
contrasts.control_arm: Same post-edited text compared with LLM-generated reference text
contrasts.reported: H1c: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -1.43, 95% CI [-1.55, -1.32]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -2.30, 95% CI [-2.46, -2.15]. Post-edited text remains more similar to LLM-generated than own unassisted text. Exploratory mixed model, Table 6: same-participant (True) estimate = -0.125, SE = 0.005, z = -25.670, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.135, -0.116]; same-participant (True) x personal style importance (Non-max) estimate = -0.053, SE = 0.011, z = -4.977, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.073, -0.032]. Table 6 labels are transcribed as printed; its caption describes LLM-generated versus human-written reference sources.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1c; p. 18, Table 6; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Linguistic acceptability (CoLA model score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory grammatical/linguistic acceptability scored by a Morris et al. (2020) model fine-tuned on expert human judgments from the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA); higher scores mean more acceptable text. This is a narrow language-quality measure, not an expert creativity rating (pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1 and Figure 12).

contrasts.reported: The prose states post-edited text is more linguistically acceptable than fully human-authored control text and reports p < .0001, g = -1.29, 95% CI [-1.57, -1.05]. The printed sign is retained exactly; the contrast order underlying g is not explicitly given. Direction follows the stated outcome comparison, not the raw sign.

contrasts.control_arm: Original LLM-generated drafts before post-editing (reference stage of treatment)
contrasts.reported: The prose states post-edited text is less linguistically acceptable than original LLM-generated text and reports p < .0001, g = 0.59, 95% CI [0.45, 0.73]. The printed sign is retained exactly; direction follows the prose. The reported contrast orientation must be checked before extracting a signed effect.

studies.label: Independent formative survey selecting personal writing scenarios

assignment.what_was_assigned: Only the presentation order of candidate writing scenarios was randomized. Participants selected scenarios where personal style mattered; nobody was assigned to AI assistance or asked to produce a scored creative text.
assignment.quote: These tasks were shown to participants in a randomized order.

arms.name: Formative scenario-selection survey
arms.description: Single survey sample selecting personally style-sensitive scenarios; no AI-assistance conditions (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 102 completed surveys and 88 attention-check passers; responses failing attention checks were not used in the scenario-selection results (p. 23, Appendix C and Figure 14). These are completion and analysis counts, not stated assignment counts.
participants.who: Prolific recruits who were not allowed to complete the main study (p. 23, Appendix C).
participants.quote: 102 participants completed this formative survey of which 88 passed the attention checks.

ai_tool.how_used: No AI intervention in this survey; it selected tasks for the main study (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

task.description: Survey respondents saw 15 writing scenarios and two attention-check scenarios, then selected six actual tasks plus the two attention-check options where personal style mattered most (pp. 22-23, Appendix C). No scored writing output was produced.
task.duration: Median completion time 3.53 minutes (p. 23, Appendix C).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper’s participant sample is stated. The formative-survey and main-experiment samples within this paper are explicitly disjoint.
sample_overlap.quote: Formative study participants were also recruited from Prolific, and were not allowed to also complete the main study.

company_involvement.description: Pangram provided API credits. The authors’ listed affiliation is the University of Maryland; no company-affiliated author or other company research sponsorship is stated.

eligibility.reason: S1 qualifies: section 4 and Figure 1 describe randomized within-person treatment/control blocks, and Table 9 explicitly states random selection of four tasks for treatment and two for control (p. 4; p. 24). The final analyzed sample is 81 people, each contributing both conditions, not a sum of arm counts (p. 4, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1). H2a compares computed stylistic similarity across different participants’ AI-assisted versus unaided writing (p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3), satisfying the codebook’s writing-diversity scope. S2 is an independent scenario-preference survey with no scored creative output and does not itself support core inclusion. Core eligibility does not establish that the reported pair-based precision is suitable for pooling.

one_line_finding: In the main experiment with 81 analyzed participants, post-edited AI drafts were less stylistically diverse across people than unaided writing (reported similarity Hedges’ g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51], p = .0002; sample: p. 13, Appendix A.1; result: p. 6, section 6.2 and p. 16, Table 3, H2a).
open_questions: The paper calls the two writing blocks randomized (p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1), but does not explicitly describe the block-sequence allocation algorithm or give sequence counts. Core coding reads this as randomized within-person ordering; a later extraction should verify the exact ordering in the preregistration or study code.

For H2 and reference-similarity tests, what exact text pairs/reference averages enter each analysis, and do permutations and bootstraps preserve participants and repeated/pairwise dependence? The resampling and independent-unit details required for pooled precision are not stated (p. 5, section 6; pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2).

H1a′ is described as a difference in stylistic shifts in section 6.1, while Figure 5 left shows final post-editing similarities. Confirm which contrast produced Table 3’s effect before treating it as an extractable aid effect (p. 6; p. 16).

CoLA result directions in the prose are opposite the signs one would expect for post-edited minus comparator; the paper does not explicitly name that subtraction order. Retain the printed g and intervals and confirm contrast orientation before sign harmonization (p. 21, Appendix B.7.1).

Table 6 labels the reference predictor same-participant (True), whereas its caption and Appendix B.5 describe an LLM-versus-human reference contrast; confirm this parameter’s coding before extraction (pp. 18-19).
notes: Screened by A on 2026-10-09 from the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-D, with PDF text checks of design, participant counts, cited results, tables and figures. PDF page numbers are file-page indices starting at one. No external paper or other screening form was consulted. Main-study n_randomized is null because 100 is explicitly a recruited count, not an assignment count; exact outcome observation/pair counts are also left null rather than calculated from task totals. The largest analyzed sample in a single study is the formative survey, whereas the core experiment is the smaller main sample. The original LLM drafts are a within-treatment reference stage, not a separate model-only study or a third randomized participant arm. Before_after comparisons refer to editing the same AI draft, with AI content still available, not unassisted after_ai follow-up. Primary flags for main hypotheses remain not_stated: the paper calls H1 and H2 main preregistered hypotheses but does not designate a single primary endpoint. Auxiliary authenticity and AI-style measures are coded other and do not independently establish a creativity benefit. CISR robustness results and exploratory mixed-model variants are retained within the corresponding outcomes. PANGRAM is listed separately because it is a distinct output-level detector score. Self-reported authenticity, usability, workload, willingness to use AI, demographic expression preferences, and formative scenario choices are not included as scored-output creativity/diversity outcomes (sections 6.3-6.5; Appendices B.3-B.6, C). Descriptive lexical/punctuation frequencies and edit-span statistics characterize editing rather than provide additional creativity or between-person diversity outcomes (pp. 21-22, Appendices B.7.2-B.7.3); embedding-model authorship-retrieval benchmarks validate measurement rather than test AI assistance (pp. 14, 16, Appendix B.2 and Table 2). No effect sizes, standard errors, sample totals or pair counts were computed. The data repository is identified as collected data on p. 1, footnote 4; no separate code URL is stated. Country of recruitment is not stated.
